title: Few people pay for AI, but those who do spend big
source_used: The Decoder (full text from the pre-fetched file)
key_facts: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) published the seventh edition of its ranking of the most-used consumer AI products; for the first time it tracks observed US consumer card spending using data from YipitData, from panels that do not represent total revenue.

Nearly half of US consumers now use AI but only a quarter do so daily; just 4.5 percent had an active paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude in August, up from roughly half that a year earlier.

The top one percent of spenders accounts for nearly a fifth of all observed AI spending, more than the entire bottom half combined, averaging about $900 a month; the typical paying user spends about $25.
ChatGPT leads the web with roughly double Gemini's traffic and six times Claude's; Claude has risen to a clear number three.
Anthropic monetizes better than rivals, with a larger share of Claude users on the $100-a-month tier.
OpenAI reported an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion from ChatGPT advertising in August.

Amazon blocked Meta's Muse within two weeks, while Shopify, Instacart and OpenTable signed official integrations; Muse hit a quarter million daily users in its first week and over five million downloads in under a month.
quote_evidence: Just 4.5 percent had an active paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude in August, up from roughly half that a year earlier.
The top one percent of spenders accounts for nearly a fifth of all observed AI spending, more than the entire bottom half combined.
The figures come from panels and don't represent total revenue, but they offer a new view of how people actually pay for AI.
why_it_matters_hint: Consumer AI income rests on a small group of heavy payers, which may widen a skills gap between heavy and light users.
event_date: a16z list published by 6 Oct 2026; The Decoder write-up 10 Oct 2026
notes: Older news re-dated: our 6 Oct 2026 edition (item 90) carried a16z's own publication of this list with the 4.5% figure and 'top 10% of spenders supply about half'. New today from The Decoder: top 1% share (nearly a fifth), $900 a month average, $25 typical spend, agent and Muse detail. The Decoder's remark that a skills gap 'could deepen existing social inequality' is its own comment, not a finding.
